rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi answers that the past-tense form, like the verbal noun, can independently convey meaning, so this distinction cannot rule out a figurative reading of the form.
rows.anchor: لفظ الزمان الماضي أيضا كذلك فلا فرق ولو سلم نقول في كل منهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In either case, figurative meaning can be conveyed through the verb's implicative meaning; whether this is called dependent metaphor is largely a terminological question.
rows.anchor: نستعير المعنى المطابقي للفظ الفعل بواسطة المعنى التضمني له ولا يبعد أن يسمى مثل هذا تبعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars favor locating the metaphor in the verbal noun because the grammatical form is not itself a word and is not an independent component like the verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وأيضا الهيئة ليست جزأ مستقلا كالمصدر وأيضا الهيئة ليست لفظا والأستعارة قسم للفظ

rows.speaker: يوسف القرباغي
rows.claim: Yusuf al-Qurbaghi answered Mir Sadr al-Din's treatise at length, surveyed several accounts of dependent metaphor, and leaned toward the grammatical form, citing al-ʿAḍudī and al-Taftazani.
rows.anchor: وللفاضل مير صدر الدين رسالة في هذه الآية الكريمة تعرض فيها للمحقق في هذا المقام وتعقبها الفاضل يوسف القرباغي برسالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi recommends consulting al-Qurbaghi's treatise, despite finding some of its arguments questionable, because it remains useful.
rows.anchor: فليراجع ذلك فإنه وإن كان في بعضه نظر لا يخلوا عن فائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers treating the grammatical form as not literally a word but as functioning like one, so it can undergo figurative transfer, as a report can be used as a command.
rows.anchor: الهيئة ليست بلفظ لكنها في حكمه وأنه قد يتصرف فيها بالتجوز كما في الخبر إذا استعمل في الإنشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Sadr distinguishes metaphor, whose relation is present in usage, from metonymy, whose relation prompts inference; Al-Alusi says that even if correct, this does not rule out dependent metonymy.
rows.anchor: وقول الصدر في الفرق : إن العلاقة في الأستعارة ملحوظة حين الأطلاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the past verb literally because opening here means facilitating, which need not await the conquest itself; Al-Alusi says the majority's account is clearer and more eloquent.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن التعبير بالماضي ههنا على حقيقة بناء على أن الفتح مجاز عن تيسسيره وتسهيله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the past form for a future event as presenting it as already certain, signaling the grandeur and truth of the report.
rows.anchor: وفي مجيء المستقبل بصيغة الماضي لتنزيله منزلة المحقق من الفخامة والدلالة على علو شأن المخبر ما لا يخفى كما في الكشاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi favors the majority's future-in-the-past reading: to God all times are alike, what is awaited is as certain as what occurred, and a divinely willed event is inevitable.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن ما ذهب إليه الجمهور أظهر وأبلغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past tense in God's eternal inner speech raises an objection: truthful speech seems to require the stated relation to have occurred beforehand, which cannot apply before eternity.
rows.anchor: واستشكل أمر المضي في كلامه تعالى بناء على ثبوت الكلام النفسي الأزلي للزوم الكذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One response says God's eternal inner speech is not past or otherwise temporal because it has no time; the author notes the difficulty of reconciling this with the eternal speech's signification.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن كلامه تعالى النفسي الأزلي لا يتصف بالماضي وغيره لعدم الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another response confines past, present, and future to created wording rather than the eternal meaning, but this too is described as difficult.
rows.anchor: وكذا القول بأن المتصف بالمضي وغيره إنما هو اللفظ الحادث دون المعنى القديم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reply treats the wording's relation to eternal speech as evidence from effect to cause, so temporal features of the effect need not belong to its cause; Al-Alusi says this departs from the apparent sense of signification.
rows.anchor: وأجاب بعضهم بأن العسر لو كان دلالة اللفظي عليه دلالة الموضوع على الموضوع له وليس كذلك عندهم بل هي دلالة الأثر على المؤثر

rows.speaker: ابن الصدر
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sadr measures tense in verbal speech by the addressee's time, not the speaker's; a letter can say “I sent Zayd” before the sending, with the imagined addressee's timeline in view.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الصدر في ذلك : إن اشتمال الكلام اللفظي على المضي والحضور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammarians' practice of narrating a past scene and measuring tense in a circumstantial clause by the action's time is closely analogous to Ibn al-Sadr's explanation.
rows.anchor: وما اعتبره أئمة العربية من حكاية الحال الماضية واعتبار المضي والحضور

rows.speaker: المحقق ميرزاجان
rows.claim: Al-Alusi points readers to Mirza Jan's marginalia on the al-ʿAḍudī commentary for additional discussion of the tense question.
rows.anchor: وللمحقق ميرزاجان كلام في هذا المفام يطلب من حواشيه على الشرح العضدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the opening as the Romans' victory over the Persians, foretold and realized that year; it also served as an omen through the victory of the believing People of the Book and so signaled the Prophet's triumph.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد بالفتح فتح الروم على إضافة المصدر إلى الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one account, “opening” is a metaphor likening the Prophet's emergence to a conquest; others locate the metaphor in its association with him, or deny metaphor and mean that God granted the Romans victory for his sake.
rows.anchor: قيل : ففي الفتح استعارة لتشبيه ظهوره صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بالفتح وقيل : لا تجوز فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi regards taking the verse as the Romans' victory as quite remote.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن حمل الفتح على ما ذكره في نفسه بعيدا جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection to the Romans interpretation is that their victory did not result from jihad or a comparable act, undermining the proposed causal explanation.
rows.anchor: وأورد عليه أن فتح الروم لم يكن مسببا على الجهاد ونحوه فلا يصح ما ذكروه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada reads fatḥ as fatāḥa, meaning judgment: God decreed that the Prophet and his companions would enter Mecca the following year and circumambulate the House; Al-Alusi calls this remote.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة أن ( فتحنا ) من الفتاحة بالضم وهي الحكومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God opened Islam, prophethood, the call, proof, and the sword to the Prophet; al-Raghib similarly mentions knowledge and guidance leading to reward and praised stations, but Al-Alusi finds this remote.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد به فتح الله تعالى له صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بالأسلام والنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “opened” is omitted to focus on the act itself and signal that the glad tidings concern God's opening, not the particular thing opened.
rows.anchor: فحذف المفعول للقصد إلى نفس الفعل والإيذان بأن مناط التبشير نفس الفتح الصادر عنه سبحانه لا خصوصية المفتوح

rows.speaker: العلامة التفتازاني
rows.claim: Al-Taftazani explains that placing “for you” before the cognate accusative emphasizes that this opening benefits the Prophet; another view says it carries the main information.
rows.anchor: وتقديم ( لك ) على المفعول المطلق أعني قوله تعالى : ( فتحا مبينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mubīn” can derive from the intransitive sense of bayyana, meaning a clear and manifest opening, or mean one that distinguishes truth from falsehood.
rows.anchor: و ( مبين ) من أبان بمعنى بأن اللازم أي فتحا بينا ظاهر الأمر

rows.speaker: الأشاعرة
rows.claim: Ashʿarites, who deny that God's acts are caused by purposes, read the lām of “so that He may forgive” as consequence or as likening the result to a final cause; forgiveness follows the Prophet's striving through hardship in God's cause.
rows.anchor: مذهب الأشاعرة القائلين بأن أفعاله تعالى لا تعلل بالأغراض أن مثل هذه اللام للعاقبة أو لتشبيه مدخولها بالعلة الغائية

rows.speaker: السلف
rows.claim: The Salaf, as Ibn al-Qayyim and others say, hold that God's acts are purposeful.
rows.anchor: والسلف كما قال ابن القيم وغيره يقولون بتعليل أفعاله عز وجل

rows.speaker: العلامة التفتازاني
rows.claim: Al-Taftazani says some Ashʿarite proofs imply a universal denial of purposes, while others deny only that every divine act has a purpose; he accepts that some acts have evident wisdoms and benefits, while universal purpose remains debatable.
rows.anchor: الحق أن بعض أفعاله تعالى معلل بالحكم والمصالح وذلك ظاهر والنصوص شاهدة به

rows.speaker: الأصفهاني
rows.claim: Al-Isfahani notes disagreement on divine purposes between the Muʿtazilites and most jurists.
rows.anchor: وذكر الأصفهاني في شرح الطوالع في هذه المسئلة خلافا للمعتزلة وأكثر الفقهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi sides with the Salaf because more than ten thousand verses and reports affirm purpose; reinterpreting all of them is unfair, and he considers the opponents' proofs readily answerable.
rows.anchor: وأنا أقول : بما ذهب إليه السلف لوجود التعليل فيما يزيد على عشرة آلاف آية وحديث

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the opening causes the combined set of forgiveness, completion of favor, guidance, and victory, rather than each item separately; this joins the Prophet's worldly and future aims.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف لم يجعل الفتح علة للمغفرة لكن لجتماع ما عدد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coordination after the lām can share its governing purpose, or can share the lām's sense so that one purpose embraces both coordinated aims.
rows.anchor: أن العطف على المجرور باللام قد يكون للأشتراك في متعلق اللام مثل جئتك لأفوز بلقياك وأحوز عطاياك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning aims beyond the main one is meaningful when they are themselves intended, required for it, closely connected to it, or follow from it, as parts of a unified outcome.
rows.anchor: وحينئذ فذكر غيره إما لتوقفه عليه أو لشدة ارتباطه به أو ترتبه عليه فيذكر للأشعار بأنهما كشيء واحد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari appears to make the lām explain the combined state of affairs alone; Al-Alusi invites the reader to determine which grammatical type applies.
rows.anchor: وظاهر كلام الزمخشري أن المقصود فيما نحن فيه تعليل الهيئة الأجتماعية فحسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stated goal is what the lām grammatically governs, considered conceptually; the cause to which it relates is what obtains in actual existence.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن المشهور كون العلة ما دخلته اللام لا ما تعلقت به كما هو ظاهر عبارة الكشاف

rows.speaker: صاحب الغنيان
rows.claim: The author of al-Ghunyān claims the lām is an oath particle, with kasra and a subjunctive verb modeled on the purpose lām.
rows.anchor: وزعم صاحب الغنيان أن اللام ههنا هي لام القسم وكسرت وحذف النون من الفعل تشبيها بلام كي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath-lām proposal lacks attestation: oath lām is not kasra-marked or followed by a subjunctive, and the proposed explanation of the vowel after deleting nūn does not help.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أنه لا يجدي نفعا مع عدم السماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the shift to the divine name suggests each listed purpose comes from a distinct divine attribute.
rows.anchor: والألتفات إلى اسم الذات المستتبع لجميع الصفات قيل : للأشعار بأن كل واحد مما أنتم في سلك الغاية

rows.speaker: الصدر
rows.claim: Al-Sadr suggests that the divine name used for forgiveness evokes God's attributes of beauty and majesty and signals that mercy precedes punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال الصدر لا يبعد أن يقال : إن التعبير عنه تعالى في مقام المغفرة بالأسم الجليل المشعر بصفات الجمال والجلال

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says forgiveness and the following favors apply to the Prophet and others, while the opening is exclusive to him; thus the opening takes the majestic plural and the other gifts use the explicit name or pronoun, magnifying his rank. Al-Alusi says this is also attributed to the Imam.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر لما كان الغفران وما بعده يشترك في إطلاقه الرسول عليه الصلاة والسلام وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi offers another possible nuance: forgiveness is attributed to God by the majestic name to suggest that He administers it directly, while the opening is carried out through intermediaries, as rulers often act through attendants.
rows.anchor: وأقول : يمكن أن يكون في إسناد المغفرة إليه تعالى بالأسم الأعظم بعد إسناد الفتح إليه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fronted “for you” emphasizes the Prophet's share; “what preceded and what followed” uses a universal “what” and a paired expression that stands for the whole.
rows.anchor: وتقديم ( لك ) على المفعول الصريح أعني قوله تعالى : ( ما تقدم من ذنبك وما تأخر (

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sin” means conduct below what is best for the Prophet's station, like righteous people's good deeds being counted as the near ones' sins.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالذنب ما فرط من خلاف الأولى بالنسبة إلى مقامه عليه الصلاة والسلام فهو من قبيل حسنات الأبرار سيآت المقربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the expression may mean what counts as sin from the Prophet's exalted perspective, though it is neither sin nor contrary to the best in God's judgment; the possessive points to this nuance.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال : المراد ما هو ذنب في نظره العالي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم وإن لم يكن ذنبا

rows.speaker: الصدر
rows.claim: Al-Sadr reads “so that He may forgive” as a metonymy for exemption from accountability, or as a representative metaphor whose individual word meanings need not be realized.
rows.anchor: وقال الصدر : يمكن أن يكون قوله تعالى : ( ليغفر ) الخ كناية عن عدم المؤاخذة

rows.speaker: عامر
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir reports from ʿAmir that “what preceded” means the pre-Islamic period and “what followed” means the Islamic period.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن عامر وأبي جعفر أنهما قالا : ما تقدم في الجاهلية

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir reports the same interpretation from Abu Jaʿfar: the earlier sins are from the pre-Islamic period and the later ones from Islam.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن عامر وأبي جعفر أنهما قالا : ما تقدم في الجاهلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An interpretation assigning the earlier phrase to the incident of Mariya and the later phrase to Zayd's wife is rejected as baseless; Al-Alusi says the reverse chronology would fit better because the Zayd episode was earlier.
rows.anchor: وقيل ما تقدم من حديث مارية وما تأخر من امرأة زيد وليس بشيء مع أن العكس أولى لأن حديث امرأة زيد متقدم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says an authentic report describes the Prophet fasting and praying until his feet swelled, and worshipping until worn, after this verse; when asked why after forgiveness, he answered, “Should I not be a grateful servant?”
rows.anchor: وقد صح أنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم لما نزلت صام وصلى حتى انتفخت قدماه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet answered that he worshipped despite forgiveness because he wished to be a grateful servant.
rows.anchor: فقال عليه الصلاة والسلام : أفلا أكون عبدا شكورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Completion of the Prophet's favor includes raising the religion, spreading it across lands, and the other religious and worldly blessings God bestowed on him.
rows.anchor: ( ويتم نعمته عليك ( بإعلاء الدين وانتشاره في البلاد وغير ذلك مما أفاضه تعالى عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path is the Prophet's conveying the message and implementing legal penalties; although he was already guided, after the opening the paths and methods of truth became clearer.
rows.anchor: ( ويهديك صراطا مستقيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says that the opening clarified the paths of truth and made its methods more firmly established than they had been before.
rows.anchor: قيل : إن أصل الأستقامة وإن كان حاصلا قبل الفتح لكن حصل بعد ذلك من اتضاح سبل الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that what is promised is true answers the preceding oath; “what” may be a relative pronoun with an omitted resumptive, referring to what they are promised or threatened with.
rows.anchor: جواب للقسم و ( ما ) موصولة والعائد محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “what you are promised” may use a verbal noun: your promise or threat; the threat reading best fits the warning context and the aim of frightening hearers.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون مصدرية أي إن وعدكم أو وعيدكم إذ توعدون يحتمل أن يكون مضارع وعد وأن يكون مضارع أو عد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid applies the statement to the disbelievers, supporting the reading of what they are threatened with.
rows.anchor: ولأن المقصود التخويف والتهويل وعن مجاهد أن الآية في الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise's being true means that its occurrence is certain.
rows.anchor: ومعنى صدقه تحقق وقوعه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats “true promise” as an adjective like “pleasing life,” describing a promise that will come to pass.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف وعد صاقد كعيشة راضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Dīn” here means recompense, and its being real means its arrival or realization.
rows.anchor: و ( الدين ) الجزاء ووقوعه حصوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most interpreters identify the promised event as the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: والأكثرون على أن الموعود هو البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath's chosen objects testify to the claim because their extraordinary character shows that the One who made them can bring about the promised Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وفي تخصيص المذكورات بالإقسام بها رمز إلى شهادتها بتحقق الجملة المقسم عليها منحيث أنها أمور بديعة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada locates al-Lāt among Thaqīf at al-Ṭāʾif; a cited but unnamed poem also associates Thaqīf with its shrine.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : لثقيف بالطائف وأنشدوا وفرت ثقيفإلى ( لاتها )

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda and others say al-Lāt was at the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة وغيره : كان بالكعبة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd locates al-Lāt at Nakhlah, near the ʿUkāẓ market, where Quraysh worshipped it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد : كان بنخلة عند سوق عكاظ

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers Qatada's location of al-Lāt at al-Ṭāʾif.
rows.anchor: ورجح ابن عطية قول قتادة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan reconciles the different locations by suggesting that several idols bore the name al-Lāt, each at the reported place.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان : يمكن الجمع بأن يكون المسمى بذلك أصناما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One etymology treats the tāʾ in al-Lāt as a root letter, like the bāʾ in the letter name Bāʾ; the alif likely derives from yāʾ because the root ليت is attested, though a wāw origin is possible if لوت existed.
rows.anchor: والتاء فيه قيل : أصلية وهي لامالكلمة كالباء في باء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another etymology makes the tāʾ compensatory: the original form was لوية from لوي because worshippers circled or devoted themselves there, then shortening and sound changes produced al-Lāt.
rows.anchor: وقيل : تاء العوض والأصل لوية بزنة فعلة من لوى لأنهم كانوا يلوون عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Several readers recite al-Lāt with a doubled tāʾ, treating it as an active participle from kneading.
rows.anchor: وقرأابن عباس ومجاهد ومنصور بن المعتمر وأبو صالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says a man kneaded sawiq for pilgrims on a stone; after his death people revered the stone and named the idol after him.
rows.anchor: قيل : كان رجل يلت السويق للحاج على حجر فلما مات ذلك الحجر إجلالا له وسموه بذلك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says a man at a rock in al-Ṭāʾif prepared ḥays and fed passersby; after his death people worshipped the rock.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد أنهكان على صخرة في الطائف يصنع حيسا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas is reported both to describe al-Lāt’s sawiq as making drinkers grow stout and to relay ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy’s claim that it entered the rock, prompting worship and a shrine.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس أنه يلت السويق على الحجر فلا يشرب منه أحد إلا سمن فعبدوه وأخرج الفاكهي عنه أنه لما مات قال لهم عمروبن لحي

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says a Thaqafi man kneaded sawiq with oil; after his death his grave became an idol, and some identified him as ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarb of ʿAdwān.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن ابن جريج أنه قال : كان رجل من ثقيف يلت السويق بالزيت

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Al-ʿUzzā belonged to Ghatafān and was generally identified as a samura tree at Nakhlah, as Qatada says; its name is the feminine of “might.”
rows.anchor: العزي ) لغطفان وهي على المشهور سمرة بنخلة كما قال قتادة

rows.speaker: الطفيل
rows.claim: Al-Nasaʾi and Ibn Mardawayh report from al-Ṭufayl that after Mecca was conquered, the Prophet sent Khalid to al-ʿUzzā at Nakhlah; Khalid first cut its three trees and demolished its structure.
rows.anchor: وأخرج النسائي وابن مردويه عنالطفيل قال : لما فتح رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم مكة بعثخالد بن الوليد إلى نخلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Ṭufayl’s report, the Prophet told Khalid to return because he had not completed the task; Khalid then found and killed a naked, disheveled woman at the shrine.
rows.anchor: فقال : ارجع فإنك لم تصنع شيئافرجع خالد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the same report, Khalid found the woman at the shrine, killed her, and reported back to the Prophet, who identified her as al-ʿUzzā.
rows.anchor: فإذاامرأته عريانة ناشرة شعرها تحثوالتراب على رأسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternate account says a demoness emerged from the idol and Khalid killed her.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بعث إليها خالدافقطعها فخرجت منها شيطانة ناشرة شعرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi quotes Khalid taunting al-ʿUzzā that God had humiliated her.
rows.anchor: يا عز كفرانك لا سبحانك إني رأيت الله قد أهانك

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said this was al-ʿUzzā and that she would never be worshipped again.
rows.anchor: فقال عليه الصلاة والسلام : تلك العزي ولن تعبد أبدا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd locates al-ʿUzzā at al-Ṭāʾif.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد : كانت العزي بالطائف

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda locates al-ʿUzzā at the Kaaba; al-Baḥr supports this with Abu Sufyan’s cry that his side had al-ʿUzzā and the Muslims did not.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة : كانت بالكعبة وأيده فيالبحر بقول أبي سفيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports may describe multiple idols bearing this name in different places, as proposed for al-Lāt.
rows.anchor: وذكر فيه أنه صنم وجمع بمثل ما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report describes Manāt as a rock associated with Hudhayl and Khuzaʿa.
rows.anchor: ( ومناة ) قيل : صخرة كانت لهذيل وخزاعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas locates Manāt among Thaqīf.
rows.anchor: عنابن عباس لثقيف

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada locates Manāt among the Anṣār at Qudayd.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة للأنصار بقديد

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda also places Manāt at the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: وقال أبوعبيدة : كانت بالكعبة أيضا

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan argues that all three idols were at the Kaaba because Quraysh are addressed; Al-Alusi notes an objection to this argument.
rows.anchor: واستظهر أبو حيان أنها ثلاثتها كانت فيها قال : لأن المخاطب في قوله تعالى : أفرأيتم قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manāt is usually written with a shortened alif; one derivation makes it a faʿala form from the shedding of sacrificial blood there.
rows.anchor: ومناة مقصورة قيل : وزنها فعلة وسميت بذلك لأن دماء النسائك كانت تمني عندهأ

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads Manāʾa with a long alif and hamza; the text cites an Arabic verse using that form.
rows.anchor: وقرأابن كثير على ما في البحر مناءة بالمدة والهمز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading the name follows mafʿala, with an original hamza and a derivation from seeking rain through the stars at the shrine.
rows.anchor: ووزنها مفعلة فالألف منقلبة عن واو كما في مقالة والهمزة أصل وهي مشتقة من النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi takes “the third, the other” as two attributes of Manāt; some say both merely emphasize that she is third and distinct.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن ( الث الثة الأخرى ) صفتان لمناة وهما على ما قيل : للتأكيد

rows.speaker: بعض الأجلة
rows.claim: One scholar says “third” confirms the count while “other” disparages Manāt as low in rank.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الأجلة : ( الثالثة ) للتأكيد و ( الأخرى ) للذم بأنها متأخرة في الرتبة وضيعة المقدار

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan objects that “other” simply means another and has no inherent praise or blame.
rows.anchor: وتعقبه أبو حيان بأن آخر ومؤنثه أخرى لم يوضعالذم ولا لمدح وإنما يدلان على معنى غير

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf explains that “the other” lowers Manāt and, by implication, the first two; Al-Alusi calls this reasoning sound.
rows.anchor: قال في الكشف : هي اسم ذم يدل على وضاعة السابقتين بوجه أيضا لأن ( أخرى ) تأنيث آخر تستدعي المشاركة مع السابق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disparaging description also rebuts the idolaters’ belief that Manāt was the greatest of the three.
rows.anchor: أنالكفرة كانوا يزعمون أنها أعظم الثلاثة فأكذبهم الله تعالى بذلك

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam explains the insult through the idols’ forms: al-Lāt was human, al-ʿUzzā a plant, and Manāt a rock, which is lowest; Al-Alusi says this does not fit every report.
rows.anchor: وقال الإمام : ( الأخرى ) صفة ذم كأنه قال سبحانه : ( ومناة الثالثة ) الذليلة وذلك لأن اللات كان على صورة آدمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi notes that the Imam’s explanation based on the idols’ forms does not fit every reported account.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أنه لا يتأتى على كل الأقوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes “the other” describe al-ʿUzzā as second after al-Lāt, with the wording also fitting the verse ending.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ( الأخرى ) صفة للعزي لأنها ثانية اللات والثانية يقاللها ( الأخرى )

rows.speaker: الحسن ابن المفضل
rows.claim: Al-Hasan ibn al-Mufaḍḍal proposes reversing the order to make al-ʿUzzā “the other” and Manāt “the third”; Al-Alusi emphatically rejects it.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن ابن المفضل : في الكلام تقديم وتأخير والتقدير والعزي الأخرى ( ومناة الثالثة ) ولعمري إنه ليس بشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke addresses idolaters who worshipped these objects while claiming that angels and false gods were God’s daughters.
rows.anchor: والكلام خطاب لعبدة هذه المذكورات وقد كانوا مع عبادتهم لها يقولون : إن الملائكة عليهم السلام وتلك المعبودات الباطلة بنات الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative rebukes them for seeing these worthless idols as God’s daughters after hearing of God’s perfect dominion, majesty, power, and command.
rows.anchor: والهمزة للإنكار والفاء لتوجيهه إلى ترتيب الرؤية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “a-raʾaytum” is generally cognitive; some say its second object is omitted and supplied by context: after hearing of God’s greatness, do they regard these contemptible idols as His daughters?
rows.anchor: وهي علمية عند كثير ومفعولها الثاني على ما اختاره بعضهم محذوف لدلالة الحال عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun “they” refers to the idols as supposed deities: in the divinity claimed for them they are only names, with no reality of godhood.
rows.anchor: إن هي ( الضمير للأصنام أي ما الأصنام باعتبار الألوهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “you named them” refers to the names; naming viewed from the name means making a name for its referent, while viewed from the referent it means assigning it a name.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى : ( سميتموها ( صفة للأسماء وضميرها لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording focuses on the names as bare labels without real referents, rather than on existing things that merely do not deserve those names; compare the parallel wording about worshipping only names.
rows.anchor: وإنما اختير ههنا المعنى الأول من غير تعرض للمسمى لتحقيق أن تلك الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes the pronoun as the three names, which idolaters used because they believed the idols deserved worship, devotion, offerings, and approach.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هي للأسماء الثلاثة المذكورة حيث كانوا يطلقونها على تلك الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi objects that denying worshipful qualities adds little; the force of the proof is that the idols lack divinity, as the idolaters themselves generally claimed for idols.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأنه لو سلم دلالة الأسماء المذكورة على ثبوت تلك المعاني الخاصة للأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names were invented by the people and their forefathers out of false desires, and no revealed proof or authority supports them.
rows.anchor: وضعتموها ( أنتم وآباؤكم ( بمقتضى الأهواء الباطلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They follow only conjecture” refers to their naming and worship: they merely suppose, falsely, that their practice is true; al-Raghib treats false supposition as one use of conjecture.
rows.anchor: إن يتبعو ( أي ما يتبعون فيما ذكر من التسمية والعمل بها ( إلا الظن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What the souls desire” is a relative phrase with an omitted antecedent; the definite article may be anaphoric, possessive, or generic, and souls naturally incline to pleasures unless reason guides them to the good end.
rows.anchor: وما تهوى الأنفس ( أي والذي تشتهيه أنفسهم الأمارة بالسوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from direct address to third person signals turning away from them and reporting their offenses to others because their crimes make them unworthy of address.
rows.anchor: والألتفات في ( يتبعون ) إلى الغيبة للأيذان بأن تعداد قبائحهم اقتضى الأغراض عنهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Waththab, Talha, al-Aʿmash, and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar are among those who read “you follow” in the second person instead of “they follow.”
rows.anchor: وقرأابن عباس وابن مسعود وابن وثاب وطلحة والأعمش وعيسى بن عمر تتبعون بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “guidance came to them from their Lord” is circumstantial and confirms the error of following conjecture: God's guidance, the Messenger or the Qur'an, should have led them to truth.
rows.anchor: ولقد جاءهم من ربهم الهدى حال من ضمير ( يتبعو ( مقررة لبطلان ما هم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Guidance” may mean the Prophet as guide or the Qur'an, either understood as the guide or called guidance emphatically.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالهدى الرسول صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم أو القرآن العظيم على أنه بمعنى الهادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause means they follow conjecture and desire in a state that contradicts the guidance that came to them; alternatively it is parenthetical and further confirms the invalidity of their practice.
rows.anchor: وحاصله ( يتبعون ) ذلك في حال ينافيه وجوز أن تكون الجملة معترضة
